summary: This standards-track memo specifies two transport mappings of the RAQMON information model from RFC 4710. One uses TCP as a native transport and the other uses SNMP, to carry data from a RAQMON Data Source to a RAQMON Report Collector. It was later updated by RFC 8996.

plainLanguage.summary: RAQMON lets a device measure the quality of a live session, such as a voice call, and report the measurements to a collector. This document defines the exact format of those reports and two ways to send them: a TCP connection, optionally protected with TLS, or SNMP notifications. A collector must support TCP; SNMP is optional.

subtitle: The binary report format for RAQMON quality monitoring, plus how to carry it over TCP with TLS or over SNMP notifications.

tldr.problem: RFC 4710 defines what quality-of-service metrics a data source reports to a collector, but devices also needed an exact wire format and a way to deliver the reports.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the RAQMON PDU, a BASIC part with a 32-bit presence-flag word plus optional vendor extensions, and maps it onto TCP, secured with StartTLS, or onto SNMP notifications through the RAQMON-RDS-MIB.
tldr.outcome: Collectors MUST support the TCP transport and MAY support SNMP, and the default TCP port is 7744. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4712 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2006. It has not been obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 8996. It builds on the framework in RFC 4710.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Real-Time Application QoS Monitoring (RAQMON) framework, outlined in RFC 4710, extends the Remote Monitoring family of protocols (RMON) by defining entities such as RAQMON Data Sources (RDS) and RAQMON Report Collectors (RRC) that perform application monitoring in real time. RFC 4710 defines the metrics that RAQMON monitoring carries in the common protocol data unit (PDU) used between an RDS and an RRC to report QoS statistics. This memo contains a syntactical description of the RAQMON PDU structure, and detailed specifications for using TCP and SNMP to carry RAQMON information.

A RAQMON PDU does not transport application data. It occupies the place of a payload specification at the application layer of the protocol stack. Two transport protocol choices are provided as options for RDS implementers, while RRCs MUST implement the TCP transport and MAY implement the SNMP transport.

The TCP binding exists to support reporting from embedded devices running applications such as Voice over IP, Voice over Wi-Fi, Fax over IP, Video over IP, Instant Messaging, E-mail, software download applications, e-business style transactions, and web access from wired or wireless computing devices. For many of these devices a PDU and a TCP-based transport fit the deployment needs, and the end-to-end congestion control and reliability that RAQMON requires are built into TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: RAQMON lets a device measure the quality of a live session, such as a voice call, and report the measurements to a collector. This document defines the exact format of those reports and two ways to send them: a TCP connection, optionally protected with TLS, or SNMP notifications. A collector must support TCP; SNMP is optional.

sections.title: The RAQMON PDU over TCP
sections.content:
To use TCP to transport RAQMON PDUs, it is sufficient to send the PDUs as TCP data. Each PDU carries its length, so the receiver can determine the PDU boundaries.

Though transmitted as one protocol data unit, a RAQMON PDU is functionally divided into two parts: the BASIC part, and the application extensions required for vendor-specific extension. Both functional parts follow a field carrying an SMI Network Management Private Enterprise code, currently maintained by IANA, which is used to identify the organization that defined the information carried in the PDU. A RAQMON PDU in the current version is marked as PDU Type (PDT) = 1.

Vendors MUST use the BASIC part of the PDU to report the parameters listed in the specification, for interoperability, as opposed to the application-specific portion. Vendors MAY also use application-specific extensions to convey application, vendor or device specific parameters not included in the BASIC part, and should explicitly publish such data externally to attain extended interoperability.

IANA has registered port number 7744 for use as the default port for RAQMON PDUs over TCP. The number was chosen to lie in the range above 5000, to accommodate port number allocation practice within the Unix operating system, where privileged processes can only use port numbers below 1024 and port numbers between 1024 and 5000 are automatically assigned by the operating system.
sections.plainLanguage: Each report is one binary block. It has two parts: a standard part that every implementation understands, and optional vendor parts. Each part names the company whose data it carries, using an enterprise number from IANA. The report is sent over a TCP connection, normally on port 7744.

sections.title: The BASIC Part of the PDU
sections.content:
The BASIC part carries a set of fields that must be present at all times. The header holds the PDU type in 5 bits, where 1 is the current version; a basic flag in 1 bit, where a zero is a valid value indicating a RAQMON NULL PDU; a trailer field in 3 bits giving the number of application-specific extensions that follow; a padding flag in 1 bit; a source IP version flag and a receiver IP version flag in 1 bit each; a record count in 4 bits giving the total number of application records in the BASIC part; and a length in 16 bits, which is the length of the BASIC part in units of 32-bit words minus one and includes the header and any padding.

Next comes the DSRC, a 32-bit data source identifier that represents a unique RAQMON reporting session descriptor pointing to a specific reporting session between an RDS and an RRC. Its uniqueness is valid only within a reporting session. DSRC values should be randomly generated using vendor-chosen algorithms for each communication session, and it is not sufficient to obtain a DSRC simply by calling random() without carefully initializing the state. Two DSRCs from two different data sources may still be the same, so the RFC recommends that an RRC use the Data Source Address, the Data Source Name and the layer 2 MAC address in conjunction with a DSRC value, and that an RDS send those parameters occasionally, since sending them in every PDU causes additional overhead.

A value of zero for the basic and trailer bits constitutes a RAQMON NULL PDU, that is, nothing to report. An RDS MUST send a RAQMON NULL PDU to the RRC to indicate the end of the RDS reporting session, and a NULL PDU ends with the DSRC field.

The rest of the BASIC part is a sequence of records. Each record starts with a record count number, RC_N, which indicates a sub-session within a communication session, and with 32 bits of RAQMON Parameter Presence Flags. Each flag that is set means the PDU contains the corresponding parameter. The flags cover the data source address, the receiver address, the NTP timestamp, the application name, the data source name, the receiver name, the session setup status and duration, the round-trip and one-way end-to-end delays, the cumulative packet loss and discards, the totals of packets and octets sent and received, the device ports used, the layer 2 and layer 3 priorities at each end, the payload types, the CPU and memory utilization, the session setup delay, the application delay, the IP packet delay variation, the inter-arrival jitter, and the packet discard and packet loss fractions.

The parameters themselves are fixed-width values: addresses are 32 bits for IPv4 and 160 bits for IPv6, the NTP timestamp is 64 bits, the session duration and the delays are 32 bits, the port numbers are 16 bits, the priorities and payload types are 8 bits, and the utilization figures are 8-bit percentages in the range 0 to 100. Text fields such as the application name, the data source name and the receiver name start with an 8-bit length followed by the text, and the data source name text MUST NOT be longer than 255 octets. All integer fields are carried in network byte order, header data is aligned to its natural length, and octets designated as padding have the value zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The standard part is a header, a session identifier, and a list of measurements. A 32-bit word of presence flags says which measurements the report actually carries, so a device only sends what it has. Each measurement is a fixed-width number or a length-prefixed text string.

sections.title: The APP Part of the PDU
sections.content:
The APP part of the RAQMON PDU is intended to accommodate extensions for new applications in a modular manner and without requiring a PDU type value registration. Vendors may design and publish application-specific extensions. Any RAQMON-compliant RRC MUST be able to recognize vendors' SMI Enterprise Codes and MUST recognize the presence of application-specific extensions identified by using Report Type fields. The Report Type and Application Length fields are always located at a fixed offset relative to the start of the extension fields, so there is no need for the RRC to understand the semantics of the enterprise-specific parts of the PDU.

Each application part holds a 32-bit SMI Enterprise Code, filled in with the appropriate SMI Enterprise ID from IANA; a non-zero code indicates a vendor- or application-specific extension. A RAQMON PDU is capable of carrying multiple application parts. It also holds a 16-bit Report Type, which vendors should fill in with the appropriate report type within the specified SMI Enterprise Code, and it is RECOMMENDED that vendors publish application-specific extensions and maintain such report types for better interoperability. Finally it holds a 16-bit length of the application part, in 32-bit words minus one, which includes the header of the application part, followed by application-dependent data of variable length. That data is interpreted by the vendor-specific application and not by the RRC itself. Its length must be a multiple of 32 bits and will be padded if necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: The vendor part lets a company add its own measurements without asking for a new record type. Each extension names the company and a report type, and gives its length. A collector does not need to understand the contents: it can see how long each extension is and skip over it.

sections.title: Securing the RAQMON Session
sections.content:
The RAQMON session, initiated over TCP, carries monitoring information from an RDS to the RRC. The RRC distinguishes between clients based on the identifiers the RDS uses to identify itself, the Data Source Address and Data Source Name, and the identifiers the RRC uses, the Receiver's Address and Receiver's Name. To ensure the integrity of the claimed identities of RDS and RRC to each other, authentication services are required. Where protection from unauthorized modification and unauthorized disclosure of RAQMON data in transit is needed, data confidentiality and message integrity services will be required, and replay protection services may be required to prevent monitoring-misinformation due to session recording and replay.

TLS provides, at the transport layer, the required authentication services through the handshake protocol, and the subsequent data confidentiality, message integrity and replay protection of the application protocol, using a ciphersuite negotiated during authentication. The RDS client authenticates the RRC in the session. The RRC optionally authenticates the RDS.

The protection of a RAQMON session starts with the RDS client's StartTLS request upon successful establishment of the TCP session. The RDS sends it by transmitting the TLS_REQ PDU. Following this request, the client MUST NOT send any PDUs on this connection until it receives a StartTLS response. The RRC MUST return a RAQMON PDU containing a StartTLS response, TLS_RESP, whose Result field is an octet carrying one of seven values: 0, OK, meaning success and that the server is willing and able to negotiate TLS; 1, OP_ERR, a sequencing error such as TLS already established; 2, PROTO_ERR, TLS not supported or incorrect PDU format; 3, UNAVAIL, a TLS service problem or the RRC server going down; 4, CONF_REQD, confidentiality service required; 5, STRONG_AUTH_REQD, strong authentication service required; and 6, REFERRAL, referral to an RRC server supporting TLS.

The server MUST return OP_ERR if the client violates the sequencing requirements, MUST set the result code to PROTO_ERR or to REFERRAL if it does not support TLS, and MUST return UNAVAIL if it supports TLS but cannot establish a TLS connection for some reason, for example if the certificate server is not responding or the server is shutting down. The client MAY send the StartTLS request at any time after establishing a RAQMON connection, except that it MUST NOT send one if TLS is currently established on the connection or if RAQMON traffic is in progress. Either the client or the server MAY abruptly close the entire RAQMON session and any TLS connection established on it by dropping the underlying TCP connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The session can be protected with TLS. The data source asks to start it with a TLS_REQ message, and the collector answers with a TLS_RESP that carries a result code. After that, both sides run the TLS handshake and every later report travels inside the protected channel. The data source always checks the collector's identity; the collector may check the data source's.

sections.title: SNMP Notifications as a Transport
sections.content:
It was an inherent objective of the RAQMON framework to re-use existing application-level transport protocols, to maximize the usage of existing installations and to avoid transport-protocol-level complexities in the design process. The choice of SNMP as a means to transport RAQMON PDUs was motivated by the intent of using existing installed devices implementing SNMP agents as RAQMON Data Sources.

There are some potential problems with the usage of SNMP as a transport mapping protocol. The potential of congestion is higher than with the TCP transport, because of the usage of UDP at the transport layer. The encoding of the information is less efficient, which results in bigger message sizes, which again may negatively impact congestion conditions and memory size requirements in the devices.

To avoid these problems, several recommendations are made. The usage of the TCP transport is RECOMMENDED wherever it is available for a pair of RDS and RRC. The usage of Inform PDUs is RECOMMENDED, and the usage of Traps PDUs is NOT RECOMMENDED. It is RECOMMENDED that information carried by notifications be maintained within the limits of the MTU size, in order to avoid fragmentation.

If SNMP is chosen, RDSs implement the capability of embedding RAQMON parameters in SNMP notifications, and the RAQMON RDS MIB module MUST be used to map the RAQMON PDUs onto the SNMP notification transport. The module defines the objects needed for mapping the BASIC part of the RAQMON PDU, as well as the notifications themselves, and additional variable bindings MAY be included to carry any application-specific extensions. It defines three notifications: a static notification for the parameters that stay the same, a dynamic notification for the measurements that change, and a BYE notification, which is the equivalent of the RAQMON NULL PDU and signals the end of a RAQMON session. All of the object types in the module are accessible-for-notify, so they would not be available to a browser using simple Get, GetNext or GetBulk requests.

Because RDSs are not computationally rich and to keep them lightweight, an RDS MAY fail to respond to SNMP requests such as Get and Set, with the exception of the Get and Set commands required to implement the User-Based Security Model defined in RFC 3414. In order to meet congestion safety requirements, SNMP INFORM PDUs SHOULD be used, and where they are, RDSs MUST process the SNMP INFORM responses from RRCs and MUST serialize the PDU transmission rate by limiting the number of PDUs sent in a specific time interval. Standard UDP port 162 SHOULD be used for SNMP notifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Some devices already speak SNMP, so the report can be sent as an SNMP notification instead of over a private connection. The cost is that the encoding is less efficient and the messages are bigger, because SNMP runs over UDP. The RFC therefore prefers TCP, recommends Inform messages over Traps, and tells data sources to limit how fast they send.

sections.title: Congestion-Safe RAQMON Operation
sections.content:
As outlined in earlier sections, the TCP congestion control mechanism provides inherent congestion safety features when TCP is implemented as the transport to carry RAQMON PDUs. To ensure congestion safety, clearly the best thing to do is to use a congestion-safe transport protocol such as TCP. If this is not feasible, it may be necessary to fall back to UDP, since SNMP over UDP is a widely deployed transport protocol.

When SNMP is chosen as the RAQMON PDU transport, implementers MUST follow section 3 of RFC 4710, which outlines the measures that MUST be taken to use RAQMON in a congestion-safe manner. Those congestion safety requirements ensure that a RAQMON implementation using SNMP over UDP does not lead to congestion under heavy network load.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP already slows a sender down when the network gets busy, so using it is the simplest way to avoid making congestion worse. If SNMP over UDP has to be used instead, the RFC points to the rules in RFC 4710 that keep the report rate under control.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 4710 outlines a threat model associated with RAQMON and the security considerations to be taken into account in the RAQMON specification. It is imperative that RAQMON PDU implementations be able to provide the following protection mechanisms in order to attain end-to-end security.

  • Authentication: the RRC SHOULD be able to verify that a RAQMON report was originated by the RDS claiming to have sent it. At a minimum, an RDS and RRC pair MUST use a digest-based authentication procedure to authenticate.
  • Privacy: RAQMON information includes identification of the parties participating in a communication session. RAQMON deployments SHOULD be able to provide protection from eavesdropping, and to prevent an unauthorized third party from gathering potentially sensitive information. This can be achieved by using secure transport protocols supporting confidentiality based on encryption technologies such as DES, 3DES and AES.
  • Protection from denial-of-service attacks directed at the RRC: RDSs send RAQMON reports as a side effect of external events, for example the receipt of a phone call, so an attacker can try to overwhelm the RRC or the network by initiating a large number of events. To prevent this, the RDS sends the first report for a session only after the session has been established, so that the session set-up process is not affected.
  • NAT and firewall friendly design: the presence of IP addresses and TCP or UDP port information in RAQMON PDUs may be NAT-unfriendly. Where NAT-friendliness is a requirement, the RDS MAY omit IP address information from the RAQMON PDU, or NAT-aware application layer gateways can be used to ensure that correct IP addresses appear in the PDUs.

For the usage of TCP, TLS MUST be used to provide transport layer security. The MIB module design helps as well: there are no management objects in it with a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create, so an intruder cannot alter or create any of them through direct SNMP SET operations. Some readable objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments, so access to them should be controlled and their values may need encrypting. SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, so implementers are RECOMMENDED to consider the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms. It is a customer or operator responsibility to ensure that the SNMP entity giving access to an instance of this MIB module is properly configured to give access to the objects only to those principals that have legitimate rights.

The TLS part adds two warnings. When anonymous TLS alone is negotiated without client authentication, the client's identity is never established, which easily allows any end-entity to establish a TLS-secured RAQMON connection to the RRC. That offers a chance to spoof legitimate RDS clients and to flood the RRC with data, so deployment policy MUST consider requiring RDS client authentication during TLS session establishment, especially when RDS clients communicate across an unprotected Internet. Even client-authenticated TLS connections are open to spoofing by one trusted client impersonating another, so validation of the RDS source address against the RDS TLS-session source address SHOULD be performed.

Every RAQMON session has an associated authorization state, and authorization in RAQMON is a local matter. Upon initial establishment the session has an anonymous authorization identity. The RRC is not to allow any RDS-transaction-related traffic through for processing until the client authentication is complete, unless anonymous authentication mode is negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: The reports name the parties in each session, so they are sensitive. The RFC asks for authentication of both ends, encryption of the data, and care against an attacker who floods the collector by triggering many sessions. It also warns that an anonymous TLS session proves nothing about who is on the other end, so the collector should check the source address too.

fields.desc: Basic flag. A value of zero means a RAQMON NULL PDU.

fields.name: T
fields.desc: Number of application-specific extensions that follow the BASIC part.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: Padding flag. The BASIC part may end with padding octets.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Set to 1 when the source IP address is an IPv6 address.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Set to 1 when the receiver IP address is an IPv6 address.

fields.name: RC
fields.desc: Total number of application records in the BASIC part.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the BASIC part in 32-bit words minus one, including header and padding.
